parties:
Prativa Rani Dey (Tirtha) ------ Appellant 
Vs. 
Dr Mohammad Yousuf, Chittagong Medical Collage and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
2. The short fact leading to this appeal is that appellant filed a complaint before the District Anti-Corruption Officer, Chittagong alleging that respondent Nos. 1-3 in collusion with each other and with ill motive to harass the appellant issued certain false certificates and with one of such certificates respondent No. 3 instituted Criminal Case No. 1(12)92 alleging oppression of woman which was ultimately found to be false. The Bureau of Anti-Corruption took up investigation of the case and they found that medical certificates showing injuries on Luna Dey alias Runa were false and on the alleged date of occurrence the medical officer respondent No.1 who issued the certificate was not on duty rather Dr. Sharfaraj Khan Chowdhury was on duty and that Luna Prava Dey was never admitted in the hospital on 27-10-1992. It is their case that in collusion with respondent No.1 father of Luna Prava Dey on the basis of that false medical certificate filed case against the father-in-law of Luna Prava Dey and some others. On receipt of the First Information Report Bureau of Anti-Corruption took up investigation of the case and ultimately submitted charge sheet against the respondents for an offence punishable under sections 167/192/198/420/466/468/469/471/109 of the Penal Code. As respondent No.1 is a Government servant sanction was obtained before submission of the charge sheet. Thereafter the Senior Special Judge, Chittagong took cognizance of the case and then transferred it to the Divisional Special Judge. Chittagong for trial and 20-7-1996 was fixed for framing of charge. Cognizance was taken under the aforesaid sections of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1947. The accused persons were, absconding and notices were published in the daily newspapers but they remained fugitives. It appears that before start of the trial on 17-7-1996 the Special Public Prosecutor filed an application under section 10(4) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act (Act No. 40), 1958 enclosing therewith Memo No. 1518 dated 9-7-1996 of Bureau of Anti-Corruption, Chittagong BAC, Dhaka Memo No. C/54/96 ChattaJ7584 dated 7-7-1996 and letter from the Prime Minister's Secretariat dated 2-7-1996 and prayed for withdrawal from the prosecution. The Divisional Special Judge on hearing the parties allowed the withdrawal by order dated 23-7-1996. The petitioner then moved the High Court Division in Criminal Revision No. 548 of 1996 under section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure against the said order passed by the Divisional Special Judge, Chittagong in the aforesaid case and a Division Bench of the High Court Division on 5-8-1996 summarily rejected the petition. Against this order the appellant preferred this appeal. 

 3. Leave was granted to consider the fact that not only that the accused persons are fugitive from justice, there being no reason in the Government order for withdrawal of the case and section 494 of the Code of Criminal Procedure being applicable the application for withdrawal was liable to be rejected and the High Court Division committed wrong following the case of Taskimuddin vs State reported in25 DLR 174 which decision was given before the amendment made in section 6(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1947. The amendment was made in 1987 by Ordinance No. 3 of 1987. From the judgment of the High Court Division it appears that there was non-application of mind while disposing of the matter and that in view of the amendment of section 6(1) of the Act making Chapter XXXVIII of the Code of Criminal, Procedure applicable to the proceedings, the decision relied upon by the Divisional Special Judge was no longer applicable and that for the purpose as withdrawal from the prosecution both section 494 of the Code and section 10(4) of the Act were required to be kept in view, Which was not done by the Divisional Special Judge and the High Court Division was not near this point of law which raised a question of public importance. On the aforesaid ground leave was granted. 

 4. The informant on 15-12-1993 lodged First Information Report with Panchlaish Police Station alleging that the accused persons in collusion with each other for illegally harassing the informant and others issued a medical certificate bringing certain allegations of torture on Luna Prava Dey by her husband, father-in-law and others and filed a false case which is Kotwali PS Case No. 1(12)92 and thereby they committed an offence punishable under sections 167/192/198/420/466/468/469/471/109 of the Penal Code and the matter was investigated by the Anti-Corruption Bureau, Chittagong who on obtaining sanction from the appropriate authority to prosecute respondent No, 1 who is a Government servant submitted charge sheet under sections 420, 197, 198, 167, 446, 469, 471 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1947, Thereafter cognizance was taken by the Senior Special Judge who then transferred the case for trial to the Divisional Special Judge, There an application was filed by the Special Public Prosecutor for withdrawal from prosecution and in-spite of objection raised from the side of the informant the Divisional Special Judge by his order dated 23-7-1996 allowed withdrawal. It appears that the Divisional Special Judge while passing the aforesaid order placed reliance in the case of Taskimuddin vs State reported in 25 DLR 174 and also on the order of the Government. 

 6. It appears that the Government decision was forwarded to the prosecutor by the Bureau of Anti-Corruption, Chittagong vide their letter dated 9-7-1996 enclosing the Government decision taken on 2-71996, For proper appreciation the same is reproduced hereunder: 

 7. Now let us consider whether on the basis of this decision the case can be allowed to be withdrawn. It appears from the judgment of the Divisional Special Judge that- the he allowed withdrawal a matter of course in view of the aforesaid decision reported in 25 DLR 174. In this decision a Division Bench of the High Court Division has held that the court's consent which is a requirement under section 494 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not necessary for withdrawal of a case before the Special Judge for trial under Act XL of 1958. It has also been held that when the Public Prosecutor who was appointed as such under the said Act at the direction of the Government filed an application for withdrawal of such a case pending before the Special Judge the later i.e. the Special Judge has no alternative but then and there to record an order of withdrawal and stop further proceeding. In that decision it has also been held that sub-section (1) of section 6 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act shows that Chapter XXXVIII of the Code of Criminal Procedure has no manner of application to a proceeding under the Special Act. The provisions of Chapter XXXVIII are not available to a case triable by tire Special Judge under the special law, Chapter XXXVIII of the Code having been completely debarred, the provision thereof cannot be pleaded by the Special Judge and the question of consent of the Court as required under section 494 Code of Criminal Procedure is not required. This decision was given by the High Court Division on 7-12-1971. It is submitted that after this decision there was amendment in the Anti-Corruption Act in section 6. 

 8. For proper appreciation of the question involved let us look into the unamended provision of section 6 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act 1958 which is as follows: 

 So on and from 1-4-1987 a change has been made in section 6 providing for the applicability of Chapter XXXVIII of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898. So from that date this Chapter of the Code is applicable in a proceeding under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958. 

 10. For the of withdrawal of a case, Sub- section 10 of this Act provides that no prosecution under this Act against any person either generally or in respect of anyone or more of the offence for which he is being tried shall be withdrawn except under the orders in writing of the Government. The prosecution therefore under this Act can withdraw under the orders in writing of the Government as contemplated under sub- section (4) of section 10 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act. In the present case the Divisional Special judge allowed withdrawal of the case on the basis of an order passed by the Government, which we have reproduced above merely on the ground that the Public Prosecutor filed an application for withdrawal and the same has been accepted by the High Court Division. It appears that this withdrawal was allowed relying on a decision reported in 25 DLR 174. as aforementioned. That decision was given on the basis of sub-section (1) of section 6 as it stood before amendment made on 1-4-1987. In that decision it has been held that Court's consent is not necessary for withdrawal of a case under the Criminal Law Amendment Act 1958 when the Public Prosecutor under the direction of the Government files an application for withdrawal and the Special Judge has no alternative but then and there to record an order of withdrawal and stop further proceeding. In December 1971 this decision was given before the amendment made in sub-section (1) of section 6. At that time Chapter XXXVIII of the Code of Criminal Procedure was not applicable in such a proceeding but from 1987 this Chapter has been made applicable. In such cases under sub-section (4) of section 10 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act an application for withdrawal of a case may be filed before the Special Judge under the orders of the Government which has been done in the present case. But the fact remains that on and from 1987 consent of the Special Judge is very much required as Chapter XXXVIII of the Code of Criminal Procedure has been made applicable. Section 494 of the Code of Criminal Procedure which is in Chapter XXXVIII of the Code of Criminal Procedure deals with withdrawal from prosecution. After introduction of Chapter XXXVIII in the Criminal Law Amendment Act the withdrawal of a case is subject to consent by the Special Judge. It has been held in the case of Syed Motiur Rahman vs State reported in 35 DLR (AD) 329 that consent of the trying Judge is not to be given mechanically. The Court is to examine materials on which the Government decides withdrawal of a case. It has been held that the Court is to exercise its functions judicially before giving such consent which implied that Court will have to examine materials on which the Government decide withdrawal of a case. The same view has been expressed in the case of Baksha Mia vs Bangladesh reported in 30 DLR (AD) 228 and Sekander Ali vs State reported in 31 DLR (AD) 134. So after amendment in the Criminal Law Amendment Act there cannot be any mechanical withdrawal of a case. 

 11. Here in the present case we have reproduced above the order of the Government for the withdrawal of the case and it appears that no ground has been shown for the same. The government's order does not contain anything that there was consideration by the authority of the materials before taking the decision for the withdrawal. The only word used for the withdrawal is "পরিতুষ্ট " So it cannot be found from this letter that there was application of mind and consideration of the materials available for the withdrawal of a case. The Special Public Prosecutor also submitted an application praying for withdrawal simply stating that the Government has decided to withdraw. And it appears that the learned Divisional Special judge relying on the decision reported in 25 DLR 174 (Taskimuddin Talukder vs State) allowed the withdrawal. This order of the Divisional Special Judge it appears is a mechanical order. He has not followed the provisions of section 494 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and he has also not considered the decision reported in the case of Matiur Rahman vs State reported in 35 DLR (AD) 329. So from the Government order as well as from the petition filed by the Public Prosecutor and the order of withdrawal passed by the Divisional Special Judge it appeal that the provisions of section 494 of the Code of Criminal Procedure has not been followed by the concerned Judge and there was no consideration of the materials by the Government in their decision. In that view of the matter we hold that such order of withdrawal cannot be supported and maintained. 

 12. It further appears that the accused persons in this case are all along absconding. And while they are still absconding the Government deiced to withdraw from the prosecution which was allowed. It is now well settled that such withdrawal is subject to consent by the trial Judge and when the accused persons are still absconding the discretion ought not to have been exercised by the Divisional Special Judge in the present case. 

 13. It is well settled that the consent mentioned in section 494 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not to be given mechanically. The Court is to exercise its function judicially before giving such consent which implies that the Court will have to examine the materials on which the Government decides withdrawal of a case. In the instant case no reason/ground has been assigned for the withdrawal of the case and there is no indication that materials were considered before taking the decision and the Divisional Special Judge committed illegality in allowing withdrawal under the aforesaid circumstances. The High Court Division also failed to appreciate the legal aspect of the matter and wrongly refused to interfere in the matter and thereby committed illegality.
